analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to count copay assistance, discounts, and vouchers toward patients' deductibles and out-of-pocket limits.
analysis.headline: A bill with 142 bipartisan cosponsors—104 of 216 House Democrats and 38 of 224 House Republicans—never received a committee vote or floor vote and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Many insurers run 'copay accumulator' programs: when a drug maker, charity, or third party pays part of a patient's drug costs, the insurer does not count that money toward the patient's deductible or annual out-of-pocket limit. The patient ends up paying the full deductible themselves, which can mean thousands of dollars a year. This bill would require health plans to count every payment made by or for a patient—manufacturer copay cards, charity assistance, discounts, and vouchers—toward the deductible, coinsurance, copayments, and out-of-pocket maximum, so outside help actually reduces what patients pay.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with high deductibles who get help paying for expensive drugs—especially people with diabetes, HIV, cancer, and other chronic conditions that require costly brand-name medications. Roughly half of people with private insurance have a deductible of $1,500 or more, and patients on specialty drugs can hit an $8,000+ out-of-pocket maximum. Under current accumulator programs, the assistance they receive evaporates once it is spent, and they owe the entire deductible anyway. The bill makes that assistance count, potentially saving assisted patients thousands of dollars a year and getting them to fill prescriptions they currently skip.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with high deductibles on costly drugs

how_it_helps.text: Health plans must count third-party payments, financial assistance, discounts, product vouchers, and other reductions in out-of-pocket expenses toward a patient's deductible, coinsurance, copayment, or out-of-pocket limit [S2][S3].

The rules apply to group health plans and both group and individual insurance coverage, with conforming changes to Affordable Care Act cost-sharing provisions so the definition is consistent across the law [S3].
The bill amends the Public Health Service Act's group health plan rules rather than creating a new program, so it changes how existing cost-sharing is calculated rather than adding new spending [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor plans would absorb more of the cost of expensive drugs, since patient cost-sharing would be reduced by the amount of assistance. Premiums could rise modestly to cover that shift. Brand-name drug manufacturers also gain, because copay cards that count toward the deductible make their expensive drugs affordable and keep patients on brands instead of cheaper alternatives—which is why critics say the bill could push overall drug spending up.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: Insurers and employers argue that counting manufacturer copay cards toward deductibles removes the pressure keeping patients and doctors on cheaper drugs, steering more use toward expensive brand-name drugs and raising premiums for everyone, including people who get no assistance [S3].

The benefit flows mainly to patients who already receive manufacturer or charity assistance, which skews toward people using expensive brand-name drugs; patients whose drugs have no assistance available see no direct benefit and could face higher premiums.
Requiring plans to count all 'other reductions' is broad, and plans warned it could complicate how cost-sharing is administered across millions of enrollees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the patients the bill targets—people whose assistance currently vanishes without reducing their deductible—the gains are real and large, often thousands of dollars a year. The cost is spread thinly: modestly higher premiums across all enrollees and somewhat weaker leverage against high brand-name drug prices. The bill does nothing about the underlying drug prices that make copay cards necessary in the first place; it treats the symptom. But for someone choosing between filling a prescription and paying the electric bill, the symptom is the problem.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee on February 6 and 17, 2023, and sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter (R-GA) introduced the bill on February 6, 2023, with six original cosponsors split between both parties [S1][S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on February 6, 2023, and to the Subcommittee on Health on February 17, 2023 [S5].
It drew 142 cosponsors—104 of 216 House Democrats and 38 of 224 House Republicans—well over a third of the House [S4].
No further action appears in the record: the subcommittee and full committee never reported the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurers and employers that sponsor health plans came out ahead. Because the bill never became law, they keep copay accumulator programs in place: assistance from drug makers and charities does not count toward deductibles, so those costs stay on patients and insurers continue to collect the full cost-sharing amount. Patients whose assistance was being erased continue to pay their entire deductibles out of pocket.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers that keep copay accumulator programs

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines in both directions: 104 of 216 House Democrats and 38 of 224 House Republicans cosponsored, and the six original cosponsors included three Democrats and three Republicans [S4][S3].

industries.note: Copay accumulator programs let insurers keep collecting a patient's full deductible even after drug makers or charities have already paid part of the patient's costs. The bill would end that practice, forcing plans to credit that assistance to the patient—which reduces what patients pay and increases what plans and premium payers cover.

Copay cards would count toward deductibles, making expensive brand-name drugs affordable and keeping patients on them instead of cheaper alternatives. That helps patients afford their prescriptions today, but it also lets manufacturers keep list prices high while quietly subsidizing the patient's share, and it raises premiums for everyone else.
Most employers who fund coverage would absorb some of the shifted cost as higher claims and premiums, which is why employer groups joined insurers in opposing accumulator bans.
